common_name: Spigold Apple (Cornell Red Spy x Golden Delicious Cross)

planting.note: Plant bare-root trees while dormant in late winter in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Spigold requires a compatible pollinizer variety and is best adapted to zones 4-8.

directions: Plant in deep, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, providing a compatible pollinizer variety nearby. Spigold was bred at the Cornell University research station in Geneva, New York, from a cross of Red Spy and Golden Delicious, combining Red Spy's large size and crisp texture with Golden Delicious's sweetness in one of the largest apples commonly grown, with fruit that can rival a softball in size. The skin is yellow-green heavily striped and blushed with red, and the crisp, juicy flesh carries a well-balanced sweet-tart flavor that holds up well in storage. The tree tends toward biennial bearing (heavy crops every other year) if not thinned properly, so thin fruit in heavy-set years to encourage more consistent annual production, and stake young trees, since the very large fruit puts real strain on branches.

common_name: Sops of Wine Apple (Ancient English Red-Fleshed Heirloom)

planting.note: Plant bare-root trees while dormant in late winter in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; best adapted to zones 4-8, providing a compatible pollinizer variety nearby.

directions: Plant in deep, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, providing a compatible pollinizer variety nearby. Sops of Wine is an English heirloom dating back before the 1600s, one of the oldest named apple varieties still in cultivation, taking its evocative name from the old English custom of soaking bread ('sops') in cider or wine, since the flesh of this apple is streaked with a distinctive pink-red color reminiscent of wine-soaked bread when cut. The medium-sized, red-skinned fruit ripens early in the season, well ahead of most storage apples, with tart, aromatic flesh well suited to cooking and cider blending, and it has historically been valued for both its early ripening and its striking, unusual flesh color. As a variety carried by some of the earliest American colonists, it also has genuine historical significance for orchardists interested in colonial-era American fruit growing.

common_name: Twenty Ounce Apple (Massive American Heirloom Cooking Apple)

planting.note: Plant bare-root trees while dormant in late winter in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; best adapted to zones 4-8, providing a compatible pollinizer variety nearby.

directions: Plant in deep, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, providing a compatible pollinizer variety nearby. Twenty Ounce is a 19th-century American heirloom named quite literally for its enormous fruit size, with individual apples commonly reaching well over a pound, making it one of the largest apples in common cultivation and a genuine novelty at the dinner table. The green-yellow skin, heavily striped and blushed with red, covers coarse, tart, juicy flesh best suited to cooking, baking, and sauce rather than fresh eating out of hand, since the sharp acidity and large size make it primarily a kitchen apple. A single Twenty Ounce apple can fill a whole pie shell on its own, a practical advantage that kept it popular in home orchards for generations of American cooking. Thin fruit if the tree sets a heavy crop, since branches can be genuinely strained by fruit of this size.

directions: Plant in deep, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, providing a compatible pollinizer variety nearby. Pound Sweet, also called Pumpkin Sweet for its large, rounded, greenish-yellow fruit, is an old New England heirloom grown for exceptionally large, mild, sweet apples with dense, coarse flesh that holds its shape and flavor beautifully when baked whole, a traditional preparation that takes full advantage of both the apple's size and its low acidity. Unlike sharper cooking apples that need added sugar, Pound Sweet's natural sweetness makes it a classic choice for simple baked apple desserts and old-fashioned New England apple dishes calling for a mild, sugary apple rather than a tart one. The tree is notably cold-hardy, reflecting its New England origins, and reliably productive; harvest in fall once fruit reaches full size and color.

Westfield Seek-No-Further originated in Westfield, Massachusetts in the 1700s and earned its confident name from admirers who felt that once you had tasted it, there was no need to look any further for a finer apple — high praise reflected in the variety's long-standing reputation among heirloom apple enthusiasts as one of the best-flavored New England apples. The dull red, faintly striped skin covers crisp, tender, aromatic flesh with a rich, nutty sweetness balanced by mild tartness, considered by many connoisseurs to rank among the finest dessert apples of the colonial American tradition. The tree bears reliably though the fruit's somewhat delicate skin bruises more easily than tougher modern varieties, so handle harvested fruit gently; ripens in fall and keeps reasonably well in cool storage.
